home.name: Francis Desjardins
home.enough: A dependency is easy to add and hard to remove, and most of what one does goes unused. The cost of adding one never arrives on the day you add it.

skills.title: What I build
skills.description: Writing code since high school, for a living since 2000. The layer I keep coming back to sits between a client and a server: a proprietary communication protocol, a real-time client-server layer, interfaces between processes, and the test benches that hold them.
skills.habits: Two habits came out of it. Cores that reach no framework, with thin bindings over them: plain TypeScript that runs in a browser, a worker or a service, and a test that fails if the core ever reaches a framework. And protocols written down first, then built to the letter in every language that speaks them.
skills.thinking: A state library and a draft engine, to hold a few plain objects, is far more than the job needs: a set of listeners and a shallow compare do the same work, nine kilobytes lighter. Some problems are the other way round — time zones, cryptography, anything whose hard part is the one you have not met yet. Between the two, a library earns its place the day the requirements outgrow what you wrote.
skills.secondary: Also: a self-declared cat person. The cats have yet to object.

work.title: What's running
work.description: Four pieces, each with a surface you can try. The names come from an eclipse: the beads of light that break through at its edge, and the three shadows it casts. What they refuse to do is documented as carefully as the rest.

dialog.name: antumbra
dialog.description: Dialog manager on the native top layer. Zero shipped UI: the renderer stays yours. React, Solid and vanilla bindings.

boot.name: umbra
boot.description: Bootstrap orchestration, and not a front-end kind: the core needs no DOM, so one declared graph boots a page, a worker or a service. You say what each step needs; the parallelism is derived from that — no flag, no concurrency ceiling.

designSystem.name: penumbra
designSystem.description: The design system all four playgrounds wear — and the page that takes it apart, one layer at a time.

bead.name: Bead
bead.description: A binary call protocol, specification first. TypeScript, C# and Rust play the same conformance files and call each other in CI over WebSocket, HTTP and MQTT 5, TypeScript and C# over AMQP 1.0 too. A builder generates a typed server and its client from a .proto. Its demo runs the server in your browser, in a Web Worker.

method.title: How Bead is made: an experiment
method.gates: Much of Bead is written by AI agents. What I bring is the ideas, the project’s values and the decisions: what the protocol should do, what it refuses, and what is solid enough to publish. Gates hold the rest: a specification all three implementations play, an agent whose job is to argue against every change that reaches across the languages, and reviews before each release. I wanted to see how far this way of working can carry a protocol in three languages.
method.sofar: So far, the gates make the agents’ output trustworthy, not the reverse. They catch much and still miss things, they need upkeep, and whether the method works elsewhere is not shown.
method.rust: Rust, a language I do not write myself, made the whole stronger. Its implementation, written by agents from the specification alone, is a third reading of it: where the three disagreed, the specification was unclear, and it was made precise. Its type system also turned up checks the TypeScript and C# sides were missing. I cannot review that code line by line; I trust it because it passes the same specification, the same tests and the same reviews as the other two.
method.author: For years I designed and ran communication protocols in my work, with the simulators, debugging tools and test benches around them; Bead, a personal project, brings me back to that work. Most of my experience is in TypeScript and JavaScript, then C#, learned by practising them on real projects. I have no formal training in protocol design or security.

home.title: Francis Desjardins: framework-free libraries, and Bead, a binary call protocol
home.description: Framework-free cores with thin bindings over them: the core is plain TypeScript that runs in a browser, a worker or a service, and the binding is the only part that knows which. Three libraries with no runtime dependencies between them, and Bead, a binary call protocol in TypeScript, C# and Rust.
home.ogTitle: Francis Desjardins: framework-free libraries, and Bead, a binary call protocol
home.ogDescription: A dependency is easy to add and hard to remove, and most of what one does goes unused. Three libraries that ship none, a binary call protocol in three languages, and the measured reason why.
